Title: Microsoft Entra Connect Health flaw exploited to steal tenant data
Context: Microsoft has not disclosed who exploited the vulnerability, how many tenants were impacted, or when the attacks first began
Full Text:
Microsoft is warning organizations that it suffered a data breach after attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Entra Connect Health service to gain unauthorized access to administrator email addresses and tenant configuration information.

Microsoft Entra Connect Health is a cloud-based monitoring service that allows administrators to monitor the health, performance, and alerts of their on-premises identity infrastructure through the Microsoft Entra admin center.

According to a security notification sent to admins yesterday and shared on Reddit, Microsoft discovered the vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API on November 9, 2026, after it was first introduced on July 23.

An investigation determined that the flaw was exploited, allowing unauthorized parties to access tenant and service-monitoring metadata and potentially modify Connect Health monitoring configurations.

"On 20 November 2026, we concluded our investigation and determined that unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata associated with your organization had occurred. We did not identify any unauthorized configuration changes," Microsoft said in the notification.

The company says the exposed information included:

Email addresses belonging to tenant technical contacts and administrator accounts.

Tenant IDs, display names, initial domain names, country codes, and regional information.

Microsoft Entra license tiers and directory synchronization status, including whether synchronization was enabled and the last synchronization timestamp.

Connect Health onboarding status.

An expired certificate previously used to register Connect Health agents with a Microsoft internal service that was decommissioned in late 2024.

Microsoft says the expired certificate was no longer in use but remained in Connect Health storage and was still returned by the API.

However, the company says the vulnerability did not expose user passwords, password hashes, authentication tokens, valid cryptographic keys, on-premises server and Active Directory topology details, or Azure subscription information.

Microsoft deployed a server-side fix on November 19 to prevent further exploitation and reviewed available telemetry to identify unauthorized API calls affecting customers. The company finished its investigation on November 20 and began notifying affected organizations.

Microsoft has not disclosed how many organizations were impacted, but more than a dozen administrators have reported receiving the notification in the Reddit post.

Some managed service providers (MSPs) also reported receiving notifications for multiple customer tenants, with one administrator saying the emails arrived hours apart.

The notification says no software updates or other customer remediation are required to address the vulnerability.

However, Microsoft recommends that organizations alert their security teams to potential targeted phishing and social-engineering attacks that could target the exposed administrator email addresses and tenant information.

Organizations are also advised to ensure privileged accounts use phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, review their Connect Health configurations, and examine Microsoft Entra audit and sign-in logs for suspicious activity.

Microsoft also published a PowerShell script at https://aka.ms/ConnectHealth/scripts that allows administrators to view the types of tenant metadata that could have been exposed.

However, the script displays current configuration values rather than the information that was accessed during the breach.

Microsoft has not disclosed who exploited the vulnerability, how many tenants were impacted, or when the attacks first began.

When contacted by BleepingComputer, Microsoft confirmed that it had fixed the vulnerability and notified impacted customers.

"We identified and addressed a security issue affecting Microsoft Entra Connect Health that could have resulted in unauthorized access to tenant-level contact and configuration metadata. We deployed a fix on November 19, 2026, and have notified impacted customers through Azure Service Health, providing guidance and support," a Microsoft spokesperson told BleepingComputer.

Microsoft declined to provide further details about the breach.

Title: A Single Malicious Webpage Let Researchers Hijack Meta Muse and Access Private Chats
Context: The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack...
Full Text:
A malicious webpage could extract a Meta Muse user's private conversations and stored memories from the assistant without triggering any approval prompt, researchers have shown.

The same attack could be extended to reach the credentials Muse stores for the user's connected accounts.

The work was a laboratory demonstration, not an attack on real users, and it stayed inside the individual user's cloud machine. NebuSec, the security firm that published it yesterday, says Muse's team has since fixed every weakness it describes.

Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched on September 8, that works through the online accounts a user connects to it and can make purchases on their behalf. Each person's agent runs on its own cloud computer.

There, a monitoring layer called Sentinel is meant to be the single gate for anything the agent sends out, and the passwords and tokens for connected accounts are supposed to stay beyond the agent's reach.

Muse's team described the aim at launch: "So we designed the system to assume the agent may be under attack and limit the potential damage."

In the demonstration, a malicious page the agent opened could pull a user's conversation history and stored memories to an external server and alter them, with no prompt shown to the user, according to the firm's research write-up.

From there, the researchers chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser, which the assistant uses for tasks such as creating PDFs, to a Linux kernel flaw, thereby taking full control of the user's cloud machine. They set out that chain in a technical breakdown.

That full control reached the credential store, the saved files, and Sentinel itself, the parts Muse's security design keeps walled off from the agent.

The compromise went no further than that one machine. The researchers did not break out to the shared server beneath it or into other users' machines.

Muse was built to assume its own agent could be turned against the user and to box in any break-in. Each of those controls worked as designed, the firm said, yet the attack still ran the whole way through.

The firm says it reported the findings to Muse's team and that the exploits were all fixed before publication. Meta has not publicly confirmed the fixes or commented on the work, and the write-up does not say whether any user data was accessed before the patches went in.

The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack the assistant on the device.

Title: Signal Blocks AI Agents From Reading Private Chats via Screenshots on Android and iOS
Context: Calling the agentic integrations into Android, iOS, and Windows an "existential threat to Signal," Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, said the move is...
Full Text:
Signal has announced that it will restrict screenshots by default to stop artificial intelligence (AI) agents from reading private chats on Android and iOS devices, but conceded that the protection is "incomplete."

The feature applies to agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where the encrypted messaging platform can detect an AI assistant attempting to read the Signal screen.

It also builds upon a similar setting that Signal introduced in Windows 11 last May following Microsoft's release of the controversial Recall feature.

Calling the agentic integrations into Android, iOS, and Windows an "existential threat to Signal," Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, said the move is designed to uphold its privacy guarantees in the AI era.

"In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that's on your screen," Whittaker said. "In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding."

"The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy."

The risk here is that AI agents can capture and store the information accessed from Signal either locally or on remote servers, with the activity occurring outside of the platform's control and potentially putting the privacy of all the participants in a conversation at risk.

Users who want to disable the option can do so by navigating to Settings > Privacy > App Security > toggle "Block Siri AI" (on iOS) or "Screen security" (on Android).

"However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts') Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees," Signal said.

"Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user's device via the file system."

Signal also pointed out that application developers lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from eroding application-level privacy. It also called out the companies for failing to provide adequate documentation about how these systems work to help design necessary controls to prevent the agents from accessing sensitive application data.

Specifically, it's urging the tech giants to provide "two common-sense remedies" to help protect the privacy of its users -

Access to easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing entirely, including screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, without making drastic compromises to the core user experience

Create better documentation and technical specifications around how AI agents function, specifically with regards to data access and processing

The concerns are not theoretical. Reuters recently reported that Muse, Meta's AI agent, was able to bypass its own official "Connector" tool to obtain access to Signal messages on both an Apple computer and an Android device by taking advantage of the broad operating system permissions granted to it during initial setup.

On macOS, for example, the agent leveraged macOS's accessibility and screenshot tools to navigate to the Signal app, take screenshots, extract text from those images, and regenerate the textual content within the Muse app. On Android, it read messages by abusing its access to the device's push notifications.

In one case highlighted by the news agency, the AI agent alerted a Meta staffer using Muse on her personal phone with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal. "This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this," the employee said in an internal post.

"We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta's Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup," Whittaker said.

"In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents."

Late last month, Apple released iOS 27.2 with an "Excluded Apps" option that lets users choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access. With Google Gemini, users have the ability to disconnect apps via the Connected Apps settings.

Earlier this week, the iPhone maker also previewed new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

Title: Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy
Context: Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent...
Full Text: Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns. Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private. "Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post. "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private. Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text. Whittaker says that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents. Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said. "Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS." Apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately. With macOS 27.3, currently in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs. "As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple said when it introduced the Full Disk Access change. "We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy." Apple is also reportedly working on its own AI agent in a bid to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. It remains to be seen whether Apple will use its operating system ownership as competitive leverage against AI firms that threaten its gatekeeping power, as it has done with web browsers. First the flood, then the dams While Apple casts itself as an ally that's helping to defend device customers against prying AI agents, Signal's decision to block Siri shows that AI agents have complicated trust decisions and the competitive landscape. AI agents are supposed to serve the user but when they spirit data away to the cloud and come between customers and merchants, they wear out their welcome. AI agents also threaten the business relationship between consumers and merchants. Amazon has blocked shopping agents like Meta Muse from its e-commerce site (though not AWS Marketplace) while Walmart has invited third-party agents to interact through its AI Gateway. Anthropic has blocked subscription customers from using third-party harnesses. United Airlines has banned transactions from unauthorized AI bots. Similar barriers or limitations related to third-party AI agents have been erected by Target, Home Depot, Etsy, eBay, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, among others. Meanwhile, there's a burgeoning industry in bot detection and mitigation, led by the likes of Cloudflare, Akamai, and DataDome, to name a few. The web browser is sometimes referred to as a user agent, based on the idealistic notion that it serves its user. That vision has been muddied by online advertising and data collection, and default settings that often serve the interests of browser makers instead of promoting privacy. Now AI agents face the same scrutiny as people wonder whether their agents really serve them or someone else. After a year or two of agent vendors arguing for access to all digital data for the sake of personalization and context, the backlash has arrived. ®

Full Text:
We’re honored that Microsoft has once again been recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Security Information and Event Management (SIEM).

As security environments grow more complex and attackers move faster, organizations need more than the ability to collect and analyze data. They need comprehensive visibility, context to understand what is happening, and the ability to act before an attack causes further damage.

Explore Microsoft Sentinel SIEM capabilities

Comprehensive SIEM across the digital estate

Microsoft Sentinel is our cloud-native SIEM, bringing together security data, advanced analytics, automation, and threat intelligence to help organizations protect their digital estate.

With more than 500 connectors across Microsoft and third-party solutions, Microsoft Sentinel brings together signals from across complex, multicloud environments. Its rich library of out-of-the-box detections, informed by Microsoft’s threat intelligence and organizational context, helps defenders identify sophisticated threats without building every detection from scratch.

Microsoft Sentinel supports the core capabilities security teams depend on, from scalable security data management and advanced detection to threat hunting, investigation, and response. The Microsoft Sentinel data lake centralizes historical and real-time security data across platforms and clouds for cost-effective retention and advanced analytics at scale. Security operations center (SOC) optimization and cost management help teams improve coverage, identify detection gaps, and make informed decisions about the data they collect and retain.

Reimagining security operations for the agentic era

On September 23, 2026, Microsoft introduced the Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender, reimagining security operations for the agentic era. As threats grow more sophisticated and security environments more complex, traditional approaches built on disconnected tools and workflows can no longer keep pace. ISOC brings security operations and threat protection together, creating a unified foundation where people and AI agents can see, understand, and act across the environment.

Through deep integration with Microsoft Sentinel, ISOC combines the full breadth of SIEM capabilities with extended detection and response (XDR), threat intelligence, posture management, and response. By connecting signals from Microsoft and third-party environments with rich security context and coordinated action, ISOC enables security teams to move beyond fragmented investigations toward faster, more proactive protection. Rather than operating as separate tools, the security stack works as one system, providing the foundation for agentic security.

Attack disruption demonstrates what this integrated approach makes possible. Microsoft Defender correlates signals across Microsoft and third-party environments with threat intelligence to identify high-confidence attacks in progress and automatically contain compromised users and devices before threats spread. This includes ransomware, business email compromise, and adversary-in-the-middle attacks. Across customers, ransomware attacks are disrupted in just 30 seconds on average.

Together, these capabilities demonstrate how Microsoft is moving security operations beyond detection and response toward an integrated, agentic approach that helps organizations anticipate, investigate, and stop threats faster.

A shared foundation for people and agents

AI is becoming part of how security teams work every day. Microsoft Sentinel combines advanced analytics, machine learning, and automation to help analysts use natural language to hunt for threats, generate response playbooks, support alert triage, analyze complex signals, and accelerate investigations. These capabilities reduce manual work and give defenders more time to focus on the threats and decisions that matter most.

By enabling SIEM and native protection to operate as one system, ISOC gives people and AI agents a shared foundation to see, understand, and act across the environment. Agents bring speed and scale to continuous security operations, while people provide expertise, judgment, and accountability.

Together, they can move beyond traditional, linear workflows toward continuous detection, investigation, and attack disruption. As agents take on more security operations workflows, comprehensive data, and rich context, the ability to act becomes even more important to helping organizations stop threats faster and deliver better security outcomes.

Looking ahead

The future of SIEM is about more than managing security data. It’s about ensuring your SIEM is a core building block of the agentic SOC, bringing together security data, intelligence, AI, and native protection so people and agents can understand threats sooner, act faster, and stop attacks before they spread.

We’ll continue investing in the comprehensive SIEM capabilities customers rely on while advancing integrated, agentic security operations in Microsoft Defender. We’re grateful for the Gartner recognition and for the customers, partners, and security community whose feedback continues to shape Microsoft Sentinel.

Title: Age of Entitlement: Privileges in Entra's access packages
Context: Attackers may target access packages with these resources to elevate their privileges
Full Text:
This research was presented at Hybrid Identity Protection Conference (HIPConf) on September 10, 2026.

Key points

This post provides technical background about entitlement management and access packages in Microsoft Entra ID Governance.

Entitlement management lets administrators assign multiple permissions to users at once by using access packages. This simplifies permissions management throughout the user life cycle.

While entitlement management disallows privileged Entra roles like Global Administrator in access packages, role-assignable groups and roles like Exchange Administrator can still be included.

Attackers may target access packages with these resources to elevate their privileges.

Auditing permissions for entitlement management requires reviewing Entra ID's role assignments, as well as role assignments in ID Governance.

In this series of posts, we'll take an in-depth look at the configuration risks and security considerations that come with entitlement management.

Introduction

This post covers the fundamentals of Microsoft Entra ID Governance's entitlement management and outlines why an attacker may target your access packages for privilege escalation.

Entitlement management bundles access for internal users and guests, with options for life cycle management and approvals. While Microsoft states that access packages cannot contain any Entra-defined privileged roles, there are still many roles with permissions that can be used by an attacker to impact an Entra, Microsoft 365, or Azure environment through entitlement management.

This series will describe how everyday access package configurations within entitlement management can lead to scenarios where an attacker could elevate privileges. Future posts will cover scenarios where access packages can be misused and share some defensive measures to monitor and improve their security.

What is entitlement management?

Entitlement management (previously abbreviated as ELM) is a feature of Entra ID Governance to manage user and guest access through their time in an Entra tenant. This is sometimes called the "user life cycle," which encompasses how a user's access will change as they join a company, move between roles, and eventually depart the company.

By bundling required access into access packages, entitlement management allows assignment of multiple types of access such as group memberships, application roles, and SharePoint site access at once. This access can then be reviewed, renewed, and revoked together based on a user's roles.

Let's say a user joins our company. Based on their persona in IT, they receive access to the IT team's SharePoint site, various group memberships they need to manage devices, and the IT Teams channel. Entitlement management combines all these needs into one access package, making it simple to onboard the user to these memberships. Once granted, this access can be regularly reviewed.

When the user's team changes to cybersecurity, their access persona changes. The IT access package is removed, and they are instead assigned to a new security access package, with a different Teams channel and group memberships. Finally, all access is revoked through the access package when they leave the company.

Entitlement management versus PIM

Entitlement management may sound similar to privileged identity management (PIM), which helps users manage the approval, renewal, and revocation of privileged Entra roles. Both tools allow role assignment, approval, and continuous review of permissions; however, they serve different purposes.

PIM focuses on assignment of individual highly privileged Entra roles to users, not bundled access.

Entitlement management focuses on assignment of bundled access (groups of permissions) but disallows assignment of privileged Entra roles.

While entitlement management prevents direct assignment of privileged Entra roles, there are still ways an administrator or attacker may work around this. We'll cover more details on this later.

Architecture

To better understand how access packages are used and managed, let's look at the architecture of entitlement management.

Entitlement management is organized by catalogs that contain the resources a user may need access to. Resources are then added to access packages that bundle multiple resources into what's required for a user's role.

Once an access package is configured, users request or are added to access packages through requests that are evaluated by policies to determine any approvals required before access is granted. Target users may already exist in the Entra tenant, or they may come from an external tenant or preapproved connected organization, based on the policy's configuration.

After approval, the user is granted access to the resources in the requested access package.

Catalogs

Catalogs are the top-level container for entitlement management. They contain the resources that users need access to, as well as access packages that can grant users access to those resources.

In the Azure portal, new catalogs are added under "Catalogs" in the identity governance panel:

Resources

A resource is any item a user is granted access to through an access package. Resources are added into a catalog and included in access packages.

Resources can include:

Group membership and ownership

Azure Resource Manager (ARM) role assignments

Some Entra role assignments

Teams in Microsoft Teams

SharePoint sites

Application access

If E7 or Agent 365 licensing is in use, application permissions (appRoles) and delegated permissions (oauth2PermissionScopes) can also be added as resources and assigned to service principals (SPs) and agent identities through entitlement management.

Resources are added by selecting a catalog, then adding the target resource under "Add resources to catalog."

While entitlement management disallows direct assignment of privileged Entra roles, roles with privileges outside of Entra (roles not marked as "privileged") can still be assigned. Currently, this includes roles such as:

Billing Administrator

Exchange Administrator

Power Platform Administrator

Azure DevOps Administrator

Role-assignable groups that assign privileged roles to users (such as Global Administrator) can also be added as resources to a catalog. This means that while direct privileged role assignments are prevented, administrators might still use workarounds to add highly privileged roles into access packages. We will look into the security implications of this in our next post.

Access packages

Now that resources have been grouped into a catalog, they can be bundled based on a user persona and easily assigned to any users requiring that access.

Catalog resources are added to an access package along with their role status. This could include group membership or ownership, active or eligible membership in an Entra role, or specific Azure roles.

Once created, access packages follow policies to determine if a user is eligible for assignment.

Policies Policies control which users, groups, or guest users can be assigned to an access package. There may be required justifications, approvals, and life cycle workflow conditions in a policy to control who can request access, who approves it, and how long access lasts once it has been assigned. An access package can have multiple policies governing assignment.

Key policy settings include:

Who can get access: Can be specific groups or identities, all groups or identities, new or existing guest users, or restricted to administrative assignment

Who can request access: The user, their manager, or only administrators

Justification: If a justification is required from the requestor

Approval: If approval is required for requests, and who approves if so; up to three rounds of approval can be configured

Lifecycle: How long assignment to an access package lasts, whether users can extend their access, and whether regular access reviews are required

Once approved, the access package is assigned to the user, and all resource assignments in the access package are delivered to the user.

Management roles

How do you know who can control what in entitlement management? Currently, this is more complex to answer than in other access management tools within Entra ID. Both Entra roles and ID Governance roles must be reviewed to understand a user's rights in entitlement management.

An overview of key entitlement management roles is provided below. Full details on these permissions can be found in Microsoft's guide on the topic.

Unlike most permissions management features, entitlement management roles can be assigned outside of Entra's role assignments. This means you'll need to check two different areas to understand who can control your access policies: Entra role assignments and the ID Governance "Roles and administrators" section of each catalog in entitlement management.

Entra roles

Both the Global Administrator and Identity Governance Administrator Entra ID roles can fully control entitlement management. This includes creating new catalogs and access packages, adding resources, and controlling access package assignments and policies.

As the Global Administrator role holds full control of the Entra tenant, this role can assign any resource to a catalog. The Identity Governance Administrator role must own a resource in order to add it to a catalog, meaning that it cannot add Entra ID roles.

Entra ID custom roles with the microsoft.directory/entitlementManagement/allProperties/allTasks permission also hold full control of entitlement management.

These role assignments are found in the standard Entra "Roles and administrators" panel.

ID Governance roles

ID Governance has several roles outside of Entra ID that allow control of entitlement management. The most powerful of these is the Catalog Owner role, which can control the access packages, policies, and resources of any catalog they own. Additionally, the Catalog Creator automatically becomes a Catalog Owner over any catalog they have created.

Additional roles allow control of access packages (Access Package Manager), assignments (Access Package Assignment Manager), and external organizations that can be added to access package policies (Connected Organization Administrator).

Unlike Entra roles, ID Governance roles must be reviewed within the identity governance panel:

Catalog Creator and Connected Organization Administrator assignments are reviewed in the "Roles and administrators" section of entitlement management.

All other entitlement management roles are reviewed in the "Roles and administrators" section of each catalog, as seen below.

It's important to review these assignments since the access packages, assignments, and policies behind a catalog directly control user role assignments.

Application permissions

Along with permissions in Entra ID and ID Governance, application permissions—specifically, the EntitlementManagement.ReadWrite.All Microsoft Graph permission—can grant SPs full management access to entitlement management. Additional details on SPs and application permissions can be found in our previous post on the topic.

Risks of entitlement management

What's the impact of an entitlement management compromise? Depending on how your access packages are configured, a compromise can be severe.

We'll cover practical examples of this in our next post. In the meantime, let's walk through a conceptual overview of these concerns.

Impact While entitlement management can't directly assign privileged Entra roles, granting membership in role-assignable groups with privileged roles is still possible. Additionally, entitlement management can still assign Entra roles with permissions outside of Entra (such as Exchange), Azure roles, and sensitive data access within SharePoint and Teams.

Theory This creates several areas an attacker with control over entitlement management may target to elevate their privileges:

Methods Attackers may attempt several methods to target these resources, such as:

Directly escalating to an eligible access package of a compromised user

Creating new access packages within a catalog they control containing that catalog's privileged resources

Tampering with group memberships to gain eligibility to an access package

Conclusion

In this post, we looked at access packages in Entra's entitlement management and how their structure can lead to configurations that attackers may want to target. We also covered how permissions for entitlement management must be audited in Entra's role assignments and within ID Governance itself.

Our next post will explore the impact of access package compromises through examples using access package eligibility, ID Governance roles, and group membership tampering.

Title: As private markets continue to grow – so do expectations, with AI raising the stakes, EY finds
Quality Isn’t The Main Worry About AI Pentesting — Data Privacy and Production Safety Are
Context: It's speeding up how attackers find and exploit them too, with time-to-exploit now down to a single day
Full Text:
AI is speeding up how software is built, which means more code, more changes, and more chances for vulnerabilities to reach production. It's speeding up how attackers find and exploit them too, with time-to-exploit now down to a single day. Security testing has to keep up with both.

AI pentesting has emerged as a way to run in-depth tests whenever teams need them, instead of waiting for the next scheduled pentest. To see how far adoption has come and what security teams need from it, Intruder surveyed 500 security and engineering leaders across the US and UK. Read on for the top findings.

Only 4% of security leaders believe their current testing frequency gives them sufficient coverage

68% of organizations deploy code to production at least daily, and 37% deploy multiple times a day. Understandably, pentesting runs on a much slower cycle. Nearly half (47%) go more than a month between full pentests on their web applications and APIs. Those figures are for each organization's most frequently tested application, so the rest of their estate is tested less often still.

Running a human-led pentest as often as code ships has never been realistic, largely because of the cost. But it means a vulnerability introduced in one release can go weeks or months without a pentest, and only 4% of security leaders believe their current testing frequency gives them sufficient coverage.

42% say they accept the risk and ship code without additional security checks between pentests

Most teams cover the gap between pentests with a mix of approaches, but 42% accept the risk and ship code without additional security checks in between. Automated scanning in the build pipeline, more frequent manual pentests, internal AppSec teams, and AI-driven pentesting are each used by around half.

Concern about the gap is widespread. 88% of leaders running scheduled pentests are worried about unmapped risk introduced between tests, and they split almost evenly on how serious it is. Half call it one of their largest unmanaged cyber risks, while the other half describe it as a known gap they're covering with basic perimeter controls.

Fewer than 1% have no plans to try AI pentesting

55% of organizations already use AI pentesting across their environment, a further 36% have tried it but not yet adopted it at scale, and fewer than 1% have no plans to try it. For a category that has only emerged in the past two years, that's fast uptake.

The largest organizations surveyed (5,000 to 10,000 employees) are furthest along, with 71% using AI pentesting across their environment. Midmarket organizations have tried it at a similar rate but scaled it less so far, at 54%.

Only a quarter see AI testing quality as a top concern

Security leaders need confidence that AI pentesting is safe to run on sensitive systems, and a way to check its work. The quality of AI pentesting isn't the main concern, with only a quarter naming it as one of their biggest barriers to adoption. The top barriers relate to how AI tools operate inside sensitive environments: data privacy (40%), safety on production systems (36%), and whether auditors and regulators will accept AI pentest reports (28%).

Asked what would most damage their trust in AI pentesting, nearly half (46%) point to a lack of visibility into what was tested (25%) or a lack of reproducible proof of exploitability (21%).

DevSecOps leads, who work most directly with the findings security tools produce, are the most skeptical — only 5% say nothing would damage their trust, compared with 19% of CTOs.

56% of teams spend six or more hours a week triaging false positives

More than half of teams (56%) spend six hours or more a week validating findings from their security tooling. Working out whether a finding is real is the biggest remediation bottleneck, named by 44% of leaders, and one in five teams spend 11 hours or more a week on it, more than a full working day.

Confirming fixes takes time too. Fewer than two in five organizations independently retest a fix in production as soon as it ships, and nearly half take up to two weeks. Until then, there's no way to know the vulnerability has actually been closed.

This is the work AI-enabled validation is designed to cut, by confirming findings are exploitable before they reach the team and retesting a fix as soon as it ships.

90% agree the traditional annual pentest is dead

Nine in ten security and engineering leaders agree that the traditional annual pentest is dead and that continuous AI pentesting is now required to keep pace. For most, it already is. Only 6% still rely on a single annual pentest.

Looking three to five years ahead, most (54%) expect AI to handle the bulk of testing, and only one in six expect manual pentests to remain a primary method of security validation. 28% expect to keep manual pentests mainly to satisfy auditors, regardless of their technical value.

What this means for security teams

Until now, teams have relied on two kinds of testing, each with a trade-off. Scanning and DAST run often but are generic by design, so they miss flaws specific to how an application works. A pentest goes deep, but it's a snapshot of how the application looked weeks or months ago. AI pentesting brings the depth of a pentest, on demand.

That changes what's possible across the testing cycle. Releases can be tested as they ship, instead of waiting for the next scheduled pentest. With findings validated before they're reported, teams spend their time on issues that are real, and fixes can be retested straight away.

For teams looking to adopt it with confidence, a few steps help. Start in a staging environment that mirrors production. Run an AI pentest alongside your next manual pentest and compare the results. Look for findings that come with proof-of-concept code and a record of what was tested. And check how your code and data will be handled before you give it access.

With AI speeding up how software is built and how it's attacked, AI pentesting makes it possible to keep pace with both. Get the full report or learn more about Intruder’s AI pentesting.

A new cyber stack, built to fight AI with AI

Delivering agentic security at Microsoft Ignite

Secure your foundations

Defend with agents

Secure agentic insiders

Changing how security work gets done

Explore what's new

A year ago, finding a serious, exploitable vulnerability was slow and expensive work done by elite security researchers. That’s no longer true. Over the past 12 months, frontier AI models have become remarkably good at discovering and exploiting software vulnerabilities, and similar levels of capability are quickly becoming available in open weights models with limited cyber guardrails. Attacks that once required specialized resources are now within reach of almost anyone.

We saw what that looks like in a single week this fall when PHP disclosed two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, flaws that let an attacker take control of a server with a single request over the internet.1 At the time of disclosure, tens of millions of internet-facing PHP services were running affected versions. Nearly two weeks later, about 29 million services remained vulnerable. Behind those servers are banks, healthcare providers, energy companies, and much of the infrastructure the internet runs on. And that same day brought five other major disclosures across the industry.

Explore coordinated agents and shared intelligence with Microsoft Perception

Turning a flaw like the PHP one into a working attack once took a specialist team months. Within roughly a day of PHP2Shell’s disclosure, security researchers had developed a working, weaponized exploit. By the following week, that research had expanded to cover additional PHP versions and configurations. The time from discovery to exploit is shrinking from months to minutes.

The physics of cybersecurity are changing, and fast.

AI is amplifying risk. Attackers can now find and exploit gaps faster than defenders can close them.

Attacks are becoming fully automated. AI has moved from assisting attackers, to executing their tasks, to planning and running entire campaigns on its own.

Agents are the new insiders. While not inherently malicious, they perform tasks and business workflows at machine speed, around the clock, and have broad access to data, apps, tools, and other agents. Like any insider, they can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised.

What we built for humans does not scale for AI. Frontier Transformation starts with business outcomes and a simple idea: technology was invented to serve humanity, not the other way around. To help organizations bring their ideas to life and innovate safely in the agentic era, we need a new cyber stack, built for agentic security.

A new cyber stack, built to fight AI with AI

The Microsoft cyber stack has three layers:

Signals, sensors, and actuators. This foundational layer is powered by sensors and actuators in Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Entra, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Sentinel, the network, the operating system, the browser, and our hyperscale cloud. Sensors tell you something is wrong. Actuators let you do something about it: contain a device on the network, revoke an identity’s access, or block an agent at the authorization layer. And because we know we’re not the only security solution provider in your environment, we connect to the wider ecosystem through more than 500 connectors. Together, Microsoft and partner sources produce more than 165 trillion signals a day,2 which, enriched by Microsoft and customer threat intelligence, fuel the context layer.

Context. This layer organizes those signals, together with each customer’s own environment, into agent-ready, real-time understanding of the digital estate that is optimized for precision, recall, and token efficiency.

Agents, harness, and models. On top are specialized security agents that work together as teams through playbooks, directed by a harness, and a multi-model approach that uses the right model for each task, designed to ensure effective and efficient security outcomes, at scale.

Delivering agentic security at Microsoft Ignite

At Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re delivering innovation across every layer of the stack. It starts with Microsoft Perception, now generally available.

Perception brings the top of the stack together. It orchestrates red, blue, and green team agents through playbooks, working together in a closed loop to deliver security outcomes. Red team agents simulate attacks from an attacker’s perspective before a breach occurs. Blue team agents detect, triage alerts, and investigate attacks, freeing analysts to focus on the critical decisions that matter most. Green team agents fix and remediate.

Perception is built to help security teams move at machine speed, drive outcomes rather than tasks, and automate while staying in control. Your team sets the guardrails and signs off on high-impact actions, and automated triggers launch playbooks when an incident meets the criteria you set. New cost management dashboards and a cost estimator help you track AI usage, forecast spending, and connect costs to measurable security outcomes.

Agents are only as good as what they can see and what they can do. That’s why we are investing as much in the foundation as in the layers above it.

Read the Microsoft Perception Tech Community blog

Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender, generally available for core capabilities, is part of that foundation. ISOC brings security information and event management (SIEM) capabilities, user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA), threat intelligence, and threat protection and disruption together so you can start your journey to the agentic security operations center (SOC). Eligible Defender Suite, Microsoft 365 E5, and Microsoft 365 E7 customers receive all Microsoft Sentinel SIEM features, 90-day default data retention for Defender data, more than 500 connectors, reduced ingestion rates, and a built-in data lake. The complete breadth of SIEM capabilities is now in preview.

Learn more about the latest updates in Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Sentinel

Read on to learn how Microsoft Perception, ISOC in Defender, and new capabilities across the stack work together to help customers secure their foundations, secure agentic insiders, and defend with agents.

Secure your foundations

Defending against AI-speed attacks starts with closing the doors attackers walk through first, and the scale of that work is increasing. In 2026, more than 96,000 vulnerabilities3 have been published to the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) Program, more than double 2024’s roughly 40,000 and more than 20 times the level of 2010,4 driven in part by AI-assisted vulnerability discovery tools.

Yet only 26% of vulnerabilities in the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog were remediated in 2025, as remediation typically extends into weeks and months. AI finds those gaps faster than teams can close them. Today we’re announcing new capabilities to help.

Strengthen your security foundation with Perception. In preview in January 2027, new AI Readiness Initiatives in Perception turn Secure Now guidance into actionable plans with shared progress tracking, helping organizations close critical security gaps, and prepare for AI adoption. Initiatives focus on scenarios that help reduce AI-amplified risk such as modernizing authentication and deploying monthly updates.

Prioritize and reduce exposure with Perception agents and playbooks. Focus on the risks that matter most and coordinate remediation using threat intelligence and business context. Two new playbooks bring together green team agents, including the Posture Prioritization Agent, now generally available, and the Risk Reduction Agent, now in public preview. Coverage spans Microsoft, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Google Cloud.

Vulnerability shielding, available in preview, helps protect vulnerable assets from exploitation by applying targeted, temporary protection to buy defenders time before they can apply a permanent patch. During routine operations the Risk Reduction Agent proactively suggests shielding when patches aren’t immediately available. During an active attack, vulnerability shielding helps reduce exposure to certain vulnerabilities by applying targeted, temporary protections while organizations prepare immediate remediation. In supported scenarios, these protections can include adjustments to network accessibility and permissions to help limit exposure.

Secure data across humans and agents with Microsoft Purview. Enhanced data classification drives precise protection with less manual effort, generally available in January 2027. Also entering preview in January: grounding protection for Copilot based on sensitive information types, which lets customers adopt Copilot without labeling every file first, and expanded data loss prevention (DLP) controls for prompts to Copilot and local agents running on Windows, which help protect sensitive data from leaking while customers use AI. Learn how Microsoft Purview accelerates data protection for the AI era.

Defend with agents

A SOC where people work through a queue of alerts by hand can’t keep up with increasingly autonomous attacks. Perception brings specialized red, blue, and green agents, and playbooks that automate common SecOps workflows, so defenders can get ahead.

Stop threats at machine speed with new Perception playbooks and agents. Accelerate threat detection, investigation, and response with new playbooks and four blue team agents, now generally available: Alert Triage Agent, Attack Investigation Agent, Detection Authoring Agent, and Threat Intelligence Agent. Helping teams move from detection to response faster, with less manual effort.

See it in action: Watch agents triage an incoming alert, investigate the attack end to end, and then improve detection rules that help identify similar threats in the future.

Stay ahead of attackers with new Perception playbooks and agents. Proactively find and validate weaknesses with playbooks that coordinate red team agents, including the Recon Agent, now generally available, and the Web App Pen Test Agent, now in preview, helping security teams identify and address vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them.

See it in action: think like an attacker with the Protect web app playbook, which runs a pen test against your app, surfaces the weaknesses that matter, and drives the fix through to your code in GitHub.

Use Perception in your flow of work. Teams can now invoke Perception playbooks in Defender, connect through Model Context Protocol (MCP) and APIs to SIEM, security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR), and IT service management tools, and bring in signals from AWS, Okta, and Salesforce. These integrations are in preview.

We are also expanding the preview of Codename MDASH, our agentic code scanner, which helps customers find and fix vulnerabilities. MDASH can now analyze repositories up to 5 GB, run in regulated clouds, and MDASH code scans can be used by the Web App Pen Test Agent to prioritize and fix vulnerabilities. MDASH adds more of the MAI Cyber family, including MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash and MAI-Cyber-2 in preview,5 improving efficiency while maintaining the quality of security findings. Learn more about MAI-Cyber-2.

Sign up to explore Codename MDASH with optional MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash access

Secure agentic insiders

Agents are the new insiders. They operate continuously, collaborate with other agents, change shape, and pursue goals in ways that can surprise the people who deployed them. To mitigate this risk we must discover agents, onboard them to management, secure and contain them, and do it continuously—even as their behavior and context change. Building on our October 2026 announcement, at Ignite we are introducing new capabilities to help customers secure agentic insiders, around the clock.

Continuously contain agentic insiders with new Perception playbooks and agents. Investigate and remediate AI posture risks and anomalous agent behavior with new playbooks and green team agents. Microsoft Entra ID Governance dynamic permissions grant task-scoped, time-bound access, while Conditional Access dynamic controls adjust protections as risk changes. These capabilities remain in limited preview.

Discover, govern, and secure agents with Microsoft Agent 365 and Microsoft Entra Suite capabilities for agentic insiders. Discovery expands by 35 local agent types, to 60 in total, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot, plus third-party cloud agents on AWS and Google Cloud. Discovered agents receive a Microsoft Entra Agent ID and can be governed with Conditional Access. Intune policies contain supported local agents on the device. Additionally, Microsoft Autopilot agents get their own Agent user account and ID, so admins can enable Conditional Access, ID Protection, and access governance to the work an Autopilot does under its own identity. Defender and Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention protect runtime and sensitive data access, and Dynamic Agent Risk assesses each agent’s exposure, blast radius, and runtime behavior. Available in preview.

While these capabilities can enable customers to secure and contain agents, they will not give them insight into how the model behind an agent behaves. Without that visibility it is hard for customers to answer three basic questions about consequential AI activity:

What was the AI asked and authorized to do?

What happened between the request and the outcome?

Can we independently verify it?

That’s why Microsoft is announcing the next phase of our commitment to responsible AI: the AI Transparency Initiative. We believe every organization should be able to see what its AI accesses and does, independently verify those actions, and control what it is permitted to do, whatever model or provider it runs on. To that end, we are expanding our participation in the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) SI Agent Standards Initiative,6 plus drawing on our own research to develop open, industry-wide standards for AI transparency, security, and governance. We’re shaping this approach with more than 40 organizations including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard, and Volvo Cars. And we will implement this work across Microsoft AI models and products, including Microsoft Foundry and Copilot.

The more agency we give AI, the more transparency we should expect in return.

Sign up to help shape the AI Transparency Initiative

Changing how security work gets done

AI is changing how attacks happen, and how security work gets done. Developers, IT, and security teams now share responsibility for building, managing, and securing AI, so Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft Agent 365, and Perception share the same signals and context. Inside the SOC, analysts need agents to defend at machine speed, which is why we’re building agentic security into the tools they already use.

Technology alone won’t get us there. Securing our own environment through the Secure Future Initiative has taught us a great deal, and our Frontier Security Engineers, services teams, and partners are working side by side with customers to put those lessons to work.

Join us at Microsoft Ignite, online or in person, to learn how Microsoft Perception, ISOC in Defender and new capabilities across the stack can help secure your organization at machine speed. We’d love to see you there.

Title: The risks of device code authentication for AI coding agents
Context: Detection and disruption availability depend on the supported configuration, required telemetry, identity integration, and deployment prerequisites
Full Text:
In this article

From a familiar phishing technique to an AI coding agent

How the attack works

One approval, four ways the impact can spread

Turning a phishing attempt into a Defender signal

Mitigation and protection guidance

References

Learn More

Device code phishing has become a recurring route to account takeover. Instead of stealing a password, an attacker persuades someone to approve a sign-in on a legitimate site simply by entering a code. The resulting access often can reach email, files, or other cloud services, depending on the account and the permissions granted. Notable earlier campaigns such as EvilTokens show how readily this technique can be scaled to do real damage. Microsoft worked hard with partners in industry and law enforcement to disrupt EvilTokens in September 2026.

That led us to a different question: what else can an attacker do with a phished device code authorization? What happens when the same trick targets an AI agent rather than a mailbox?

We used GitHub Copilot CLI as an illustrative example. Depending on its configuration, it can work with code, run commands on a user’s machine, retain context across sessions, and allow an active session to be steered remotely. Like many command-line tools, it supports the OAuth device flow for sign-in. The phishing technique itself is not specific to GitHub or Copilot CLI: any public client that supports the device flow can be abused the same way, and the attacker chooses the requested scopes when starting the flow.

We explored this scenario in a controlled lab simulation. A victim test account approved a GitHub device-code request initiated by an attacker client we controlled. With that approval, we were able to analyze four possible outcomes:

Steer an active Copilot CLI session remotely, if the user has enabled remote control and organization policy allows it, and, subject to local permissions and approval settings, have the agent run commands on the user’s machine.

Add misleading entries to the agent’s memory that could influence later interactions.

Read Copilot CLI sessions that were synchronized to the cloud.

Access private repositories available to the affected account.

These are proof-of-concept results showing how existing features, working as designed, could be abused after a phished authorization; they are not attacks we have observed in the wild. These outcomes require the victim user to approve a device code request initiated by the attacker; each outcome also depends on the account permissions and enabled features described below.

Later in this post, we show how Microsoft Defender helps detect these attacks by connecting phishing attempts with GitHub authentication activity, and how organizations can disrupt suspicious access to protect affected identities.

From a familiar phishing technique to an AI coding agent

The OAuth device flow helps clients such as command-line tools sign in without displaying a full browser. A client requests a short code; the user enters it on the service’s verification page; the requesting client receives access after approval. In device code phishing, the attacker starts the request and persuades someone else to approve it.

Microsoft has reported device code phishing against accounts in several campaigns, including Storm-2372, an AI-enabled campaign in 2026, and EvilTokens. Those cases motivated us to examine a different target: a coding agent that can work with repositories and, when remote control is enabled, expose an active session to remote interaction.

The remainder of this post describes a controlled GitHub Copilot CLI simulation; we have not observed the four outcomes below in those campaigns or in the wild.

How the attack works

Figure 1. A user approves a legitimate GitHub device-code request that was initiated by the attacker-controlled client. Conceptual illustration.

Initiate: The attacker starts a device-code sign-in request. In our simulation, we used the Copilot CLI client, but any device-flow client could be used.

Lure: The attacker sends the short code and GitHub verification link to the user, for example under the pretext of an IT request or a Copilot license check. The verification page is genuinely hosted by GitHub; the legitimate domain alone does not establish who initiated the request.

Approve: The user opens the GitHub page, signs in if needed, and approves the request. This is the social engineering step.

Sign in: After approval, the attacker-controlled client completes the sign-in automatically.

Operate: The attacker can act within the permissions granted to the application and the resources available to the affected account.

The request behind the code

The following example shows the initial HTTP request to GitHub’s device authorization endpoint. The Copilot CLI client identifier is public; it is not a client secret. The attacker sends the short code returned by GitHub to the user. Once the user approves it, the requesting client signs in without another manual step.

GitHub Device Code Authentication (Simplified) Endpoint: GitHub Device Authorization Endpoint Client ID: Requested scopes:

The request looks legitimate

The user signs in on the real GitHub site, not a lookalike page. A familiar domain therefore cannot tell the user whether the request was theirs. An authorization also appears under a legitimate application name; the name alone cannot distinguish the attacker-controlled client from an expected sign-in.

One approval, four ways the impact can spread

The device code approval was only the starting point. What an attacker could do next depended on the account’s permissions, enabled features, memory settings, and whether an active session could be controlled remotely.

Figure 2. Four possible outcomes in the lab, each subject to the account’s permissions and enabled features. Conceptual illustration.

1. An attacker can steer an enabled remote session

Copilot CLI supports remote steering of an active interactive session when the user has enabled remote control for that session and organization policy allows it. In our lab, the attacker-controlled client used the test account’s authorization to interact with a remotely controllable session. The agent ran a command on the test machine, subject to the session’s approval prompts and local operating-system permissions. This demonstrates misuse of an authorized remote-session capability working as designed; it is not unauthenticated remote code execution and does not apply when remote control is disabled, the session is not running, or the machine is offline.

Figure 3. Remote-session misuse is bounded by the local machine’s permissions and approval controls. Conceptual illustration.

2. Memory can carry the attack forward

Copilot Memory can retain repository facts and user preferences. In the simulation, we added misleading entries using the agent’s /memory command. If those entries are used in later interactions, the effects can outlast the initial sign-in. The behavior depends on which memory features and policies are enabled.

Figure 4. Misleading memory can affect later agent interactions. Conceptual illustration.

3. Synced sessions reveal earlier context

Where cloud session storage is enabled, we could read the test account’s synced Copilot CLI sessions, including sessions from before the simulation. They may contain code snippets, file paths, architecture discussions, and other work context. For Copilot Business and Enterprise, availability depends on the organization’s session-storage policy; syncing a session does not itself enable remote control.

4. Repository access follows the account

In the lab, the authorization let us access private repositories available to the test account. The request included the repo scope along with read:user, read:org, gist, and codespace. These scopes are chosen by the client that starts the flow; the resulting repository access reflects the requested scopes and the account’s permissions, not a property of Copilot CLI itself. The potential exposure is bounded by the account’s repository access, which can include application code and infrastructure definitions.

A phishing message, a click, and a GitHub authorization can each look unremarkable on their own. The challenge for defenders is recognizing when they belong to the same attempted takeover. The legitimate verification page is part of the story, not evidence that the request was safe.

Turning a phishing attempt into a Defender signal

Microsoft Defender helps organizations detect and respond to device code phishing targeting GitHub accounts. With the GitHub Enterprise Cloud connector enabled in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, organizations gain visibility into GitHub activity that can support investigations of suspicious authorization patterns.

As part of our research, we developed two detections for suspected GitHub Copilot CLI device code phishing, covering attacks delivered through email and Microsoft Teams.

These detections correlate suspicious messages and clicks with subsequent GitHub OAuth token creation and regeneration events, helping identify potentially unauthorized Copilot CLI authorizations that might otherwise appear legitimate. Microsoft Defender XDR customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below.

Microsoft Defender coverage

Observed activity

Tactic

Microsoft Defender XDR: Suspected GitHub Copilot CLI device code phishing via email

Suspected device code phishing delivered through email, potentially resulting in unauthorized GitHub Copilot CLI access.

Initial Access / Credential Access

Microsoft Defender XDR: Suspected GitHub Copilot CLI device code phishing via Microsoft Teams

Suspected device code phishing delivered through Microsoft Teams, potentially resulting in unauthorized GitHub Copilot CLI access

Initial Access / Credential Access

Beyond detection, we also developed a disruption action for GitHub Enterprise Managed Users (EMU). This action suspends the affected managed identity through the organization’s identity provider, interrupting the attacker’s access. We validated this capability in our research environment.

Responders should also review and revoke unexpected OAuth authorizations, verify that access is blocked, and investigate potentially affected sessions, repositories, and saved memory.

Together, these capabilities help security teams move from identifying a potential phishing attempt to containing the affected identity. Detection and disruption availability depend on the supported configuration, required telemetry, identity integration, and deployment prerequisites.

Figure 5. Microsoft Defender alert generated for suspected GitHub Copilot CLI device code phishing via email. Figure 6. Research model for identifying and containing the affected managed identity. Conceptual illustration.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Make the approval rule clear to everyone who uses developer and AI tools: enter a device code only for a sign-in you initiated yourself. An unexpected request to “verify” GitHub or activate Copilot should be treated as a phishing attempt, even if the page is hosted on github.com. GitHub’s own verification page warns users never to use a code sent by someone else.

Configure Safe Links policies in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 for email and verify Safe Links protection for Microsoft Teams. These protections can help with malicious links and provide investigation context; a legitimate GitHub verification URL still requires the user to recognize an unsolicited code request.

Review GitHub Copilot CLI session settings. For organization-provided seats, GitHub’s “Store local sessions in the Cloud” policy determines whether sessions can be stored and remotely controlled. Choose the least permissive setting that supports your workflows. Remote control also requires an active, online interactive session.

Review authorized OAuth applications in GitHub account settings and revoke authorizations that are unexpected or no longer needed. Limit repository access with appropriate organization roles so an affected account cannot reach more code than its work requires.

If Copilot Memory is enabled, use GitHub’s memory-management controls to review and remove suspicious repository facts or user preferences. Disabling memory does not automatically delete entries already stored, so review the saved content during incident response.

Connect GitHub Enterprise Cloud to Defender for Cloud Apps and validate the activity available in your environment before relying on it for investigations.

Remember: A legitimate sign-in can still be the wrong one

The most striking part of this simulation was how little needed to look suspicious. The user visited the real GitHub site and approved a normal-looking request. Yet the approval belonged to a client the user had not started. From there, the consequences depended on what that identity could access and which Copilot CLI capabilities were enabled.

That is why this is more than a story about a code. As AI agents gain access to repositories, session history, and local tools, the impact of a phished authorization increasingly depends on what those agents can reach.

A legitimate verification page does not mean the request is safe. Users should approve only device-code requests they initiated. Organizations should regularly review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorizations, restrict Copilot session and memory settings to what their workflows require, and validate GitHub activity visibility in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps to support investigations.

Ultimately, protecting against device code phishing requires both user awareness and the ability to connect suspicious authorization activity to the phishing attempt that preceded it.

MITRE ATT&CK techniques observed

These mappings describe behaviors demonstrated in the proof-of-concept simulation, not an attributed campaign.

T1566.002 – Phishing: Spearphishing Link (Initial Access). In the tested email delivery, a link led the user to the device authorization page and prompted approval.

T1528 – Steal Application Access Token (Credential Access). After the test account approved the request, the attacker-controlled client obtained an OAuth token.

Full Text:
Microsoft Defender sees a huge amount of attacker activity, and if you run Microsoft 365 E5 or Defender Suite for Business Premium, you're already paying for that visibility. But when Defender flags a potential attack, someone has to open the incident, understand what happened, and decide how to respond while the attacker is still inside.

That someone can now be the Huntress SOC. Through an expanded integration, Huntress now ingests incidents from across the entire Microsoft Defender ecosystem so our analysts can investigate what Defender finds, determine whether there's an active threat, and respond to the attack. Your team gets 24/7 SOC support for Microsoft security tools, without having to investigate and respond to those incidents on your own.

"We integrate with the Microsoft Defender Suite because organizations of every size need Defense in Depth, and the signals Microsoft customers already own are another layer that makes that defense stronger. The results are already real: Defender Suite signal + Huntress detections, combined, uncovered a token-replay campaign that compromised 97 accounts across 79 organizations. That's what defense in depth looks like: all layers working together."

Adam Bates, Vice President of Product Management, Huntress

Full Defender Ecosystem Visibility Actioned By The Huntress SOC

Huntress has always leveraged Microsoft signals from Defender for Endpoint and Microsoft Defender Antivirus. Now, the Huntress platform has expanded our integration to bring the rest of the Defender suite along.

Defender for Identity, Defender for Office 365, Defender for Cloud Apps, and Entra ID Protection all send incident data and context to the Huntress Agentic Security Platform. A phishing email caught by Office 365, a risky OAuth app flagged by Cloud Apps, and a compromised-account verdict from Entra ID Protection all land in front of an analyst, even when no device is involved. Your team doesn't stitch these signals together or sort the queue by severity. Our SOC does that, then sends you a report that says what happened and what we did about it.

Expanded Detections to Catch More Attacks

When an attacker replays a stolen session token, no machine in your environment does anything wrong. The target is the account. That's typical of what Defender sees: 85% of medium- and high-severity incidents in a recent two-week period had no device-related evidence at all. So Huntress doesn't wait for a hostname. Each incident goes on the endpoints it involves, the protected identities it names, or both.

A Defender incident tells you what Microsoft concluded, but our analysts want to know what else happened. Using Defender's advanced hunting, the SOC can query the raw data in your own Microsoft tenant, going back as far as 30 days. An analyst can pull the process tree from the machine behind a credential theft alert, check whether the same tool turned up on other devices, or follow a suspicious sign-in to see what that account did next. Huntress sets its own per-tenant query limits so our hunting never eats into the Microsoft quota your other tools share. What you get back is a report built on what happened in your environment.

Real-world results that have already protected organizations

We've already put Huntress and Microsoft data to work against real attackers.

From July 14 to September 22, 2026, Huntress tracked a token-replay campaign targeting Microsoft 365 accounts across 79 organizations. The campaign was first surfaced by a Microsoft alert, backed by intelligence from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center (MSTIC). Attackers used techniques including adversary-in-the-middle phishing, where a fake sign-in page relays the victim's login to Microsoft and captures the session token issued after they complete MFA. By replaying that token, the attackers could access the account without entering a password or completing another MFA prompt.

WHAT HUNTRESS FOUND

Figure 1: Overall statistics of the activity Huntress observed

The attackers gained access to accounts without compromising customer endpoints. Once inside, they registered rogue devices and their own authenticator apps to maintain access, then created inbox rules to hide their communications from the account owners. In one case, an attacker used a hijacked mailbox to send a payroll-related email to an outside accountant and hid the accountant's replies, giving the victim little chance to spot the exchange.

Huntress Managed ITDR detections first identified the activity, while Microsoft Entra ID Protection independently flagged the same attacker infrastructure as known threat actor IP addresses across multiple customer environments. Those Microsoft signals gave our analysts additional context on the activity they were already investigating, showing how the two sources can support the same investigation.

This campaign is the reason we rebuilt the pipeline. It now attaches incidents like these to identities and signals every affected account, including when one incident names several of them.

If you suspect a token replay compromise, revoke the user's sessions and reset the password. A reset alone leaves attacker-registered devices and MFA methods in place, so audit both in Entra ID afterward.

One more way Huntress strengthens your Microsoft security

Huntress has been helping organizations get more from their Microsoft security for a while now. This integration adds to what's already in place:

Investigating and responding to signals from Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and Microsoft Defender Antivirus, paired with Huntress's own endpoint telemetry. Because Huntress runs its own agent, the SOC can contain and remediate on the machine itself and doesn't stop at filing a ticket.

Managed ISPM hardens Microsoft 365 environments to protect against misconfigurations and over-privileged accounts before an attacker can use them as a way in. It helps organizations implement best-practice controls and Conditional Access Policies, stay ahead of configuration drift through continuous enforcement, and improve their Microsoft Secure Score.

Managed ITDR stops identity attacks in Microsoft 365 as they unfold, to deliver identity protection for attacks like credential theft, session hijacking and rogue OAuth apps. Its new Adversary Infrastructure capability takes one organization's incident and turns it into a Conditional Access block across every eligible, opted-in P1 tenant the same day.
